q: Felix Candela's Xochimilco Restaurant (1958), known for its thin concrete-shell 'umbrella' roof, is located in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Concrete
n: Candela's restaurant in Xochimilco, part of Mexico City, uses hyperbolic paraboloid concrete shells to create a dramatic, thin, umbrella-like roof.

q: Jacques-Germain Soufflot's Church of Sainte-Genevieve (1755–1792), with its grand columned portico, was built in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Column
n: Soufflot's Church of Sainte-Genevieve in Paris, later converted into the Pantheon, is a major Neo-Classical building inspired by ancient Roman and Greek columned temples.

q: Joseph Paxton's Crystal Palace, built almost entirely of cast iron and glass, was erected for London's Great Exhibition in which year?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Glass
n: The Crystal Palace (1851) used vast sheets of glass set in a cast-iron frame, making it one of the earliest large-scale glass-and-iron buildings.

q: The Market of Trajan, an early multi-level arched shopping and administrative complex, was built in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Arch
n: Built in the AD 100s, the Market of Trajan in Rome is often cited as one of the world's earliest shopping-center-like complexes, relying heavily on the arch.

q: Benjamin Latrobe, credited with the columned design of the United States Capitol (1803–1820s), worked in which architectural style?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Column
n: Latrobe's work on the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., beginning in 1803, exemplifies Neo-Classical Architecture, drawing on ancient Greek and Roman columned forms.

q: Which of these wooden structures predates the others by several centuries, dating to around AD 711?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Wood
n: The Horyu-ji shrine in Japan, dating to about AD 711, is centuries older than the Borgund Stave Church or the Forbidden City Complex.

q: Richard Buckminster Fuller's Dymaxion House (1945), an early geodesic-influenced dwelling, is now preserved at which museum?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: Fuller's prototype Dymaxion House is preserved at the Henry Ford Museum in Dearborn, Michigan, reflecting his interest in efficient, lightweight domed and dome-like structures.

q: The prehistoric stone village of Skara Brae, remarkably preserved with built-in stone furniture, is located in which island group?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Stone
n: Skara Brae, dating to around 3100 BC, sits in the Orkney Islands off Scotland and preserves stone beds, dressers, and hearths from its Neolithic inhabitants.

q: As a structural system, Stonehenge is a key early example of which construction method, using upright stones topped by horizontal ones?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Post-and-Lintel
n: Stonehenge's uprights topped by horizontal lintel stones make it a classic prehistoric example of post-and-lintel construction, one of the oldest structural systems.

q: Which two of these both used cast iron and were designed by architects working in Paris around the mid-to-late 1800s?
o: Marshall Field Warehouse and Severn River Bridge
The Eiffel Tower and Crystal Palace
Crystal Palace and Marshall Field Warehouse
The Reading Room of the Bibliotheque Sainte-Genevieve and the Paris Opera
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Cast Iron
n: Both Labrouste's Bibliotheque Sainte-Genevieve reading room (1840s) and Garnier's Paris Opera (1860s) were built in Paris and made structural use of cast iron.

q: The geodesic dome popularized by Buckminster Fuller was showcased at the 1960s World's Fair held in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: Fuller's geodesic dome for the United States Pavilion appeared at Expo '67 in Montreal, becoming one of the most famous geodesic structures ever built.

q: The Parthenon, the great Doric temple on the Acropolis of Athens, was completed in roughly which years?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Column
n: The Parthenon was completed 447–438 BC as the centerpiece of the Athenian Acropolis, a defining monument of Ancient Greek Architecture.

q: Taos Pueblo, a multi-story adobe brick settlement still inhabited today, is found in which US state?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: Taos Pueblo, dating to around the 1450s, is located in New Mexico and is one of the oldest continuously inhabited communities in the United States.

q: The Galla Placidia Mausoleum, an early Christian brick structure famous for its mosaics, is located in which Italian city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: Built around AD 425 in Ravenna, the Galla Placidia Mausoleum is a small cross-shaped brick building renowned for its deep-blue interior mosaics.

q: Robert Venturi's Guild House (1963), an early and influential work of postmodern architecture, was built in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: Guild House, a senior-citizens' residence in Philadelphia, is often cited as one of the first buildings to break from strict modernist orthodoxy, incorporating ordinary brick and historical allusion.

q: The Baths of Caracalla in Rome, which relied heavily on the arch for its vaulted bathing halls, date to roughly which year?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Arch
n: Completed around AD 211, the Baths of Caracalla used extensive arched and vaulted construction typical of Ancient Roman engineering.

q: Richard Boyle designed the domed Chiswick House in the 1720s, in which architectural style?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: Chiswick House, designed by Richard Boyle (1695–1753) in West London, is a Neo-Classical villa directly inspired by Palladio's earlier domed designs.

q: Which Roman structure used massive concrete arches and vaults to create a soaring interior space still visible today in the Roman Forum?
o: The Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Arch
n: The Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine (c. AD 310) used massive concrete arches and vaults to span its enormous central hall, remnants of which still stand in the Roman Forum.

q: Which Roman structure is known for both its interior marble cladding and its unreinforced concrete dome?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: The Pantheon in Rome combines marble interior facing with its famous unreinforced concrete dome, making it a landmark for both materials.

q: The Baths of Caracalla, a large brick-and-concrete bathing complex, were built in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: The Baths of Caracalla (c. AD 211) were an enormous public bathing complex in Rome, a showcase of Ancient Roman brick-faced concrete construction.

q: The Buddhist Shrine at Horyu-ji, among the world's oldest surviving wooden buildings, is located in which country?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Wood
n: Dating to around AD 711, the Horyu-ji shrine complex in Japan contains some of the oldest wooden structures still standing anywhere in the world.

q: Roughly when was Jericho first fortified with brick walls, making it one of the earliest known walled settlements?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: Jericho's brick fortifications date to roughly 7000 BC, placing it among the very earliest walled towns in the Ancient Near East.

q: Thomas Jefferson designed his own domed home, Monticello, in the 1770s, located in which state?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: Jefferson's Monticello, near Charlottesville, Virginia, applies Neo-Classical principles and a shallow dome inspired by his admiration for Roman and Palladian architecture.

q: Catal Huyuk, an early brick settlement studied for its densely packed mudbrick houses, was located in which region?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: Catal Huyuk sits in western Turkey (Anatolia) and dates to roughly 6500 BC, part of the broader Ancient Near Eastern building tradition.

q: Benjamin Henry Latrobe began work on the domed United States Capitol in Washington, D.C., in which year?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: Latrobe began the Capitol's Neo-Classical design, including its domed elements, in 1803, though the building was expanded and altered by later architects.

q: The glazed-brick Ishtar Gate of Babylon dates to roughly which period?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: The Ishtar Gate was built around 575 BC under the Neo-Babylonian empire and was famed for its blue glazed bricks decorated with animal reliefs.

q: Louis Sullivan designed the Wainwright Building, an early brick-clad steel-frame skyscraper, in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: Completed in 1891, Sullivan's Wainwright Building stands in St. Louis and is considered a pioneering statement of the modern tall office building, expressed partly in brick and terracotta cladding.

q: The Great Mosque of Djenne, one of the world's largest mudbrick (adobe) buildings, is located in which country?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: The Great Mosque of Djenne, rebuilt in its current form in the 1200s tradition, stands in Mali and is a landmark of Sudano-Sahelian mudbrick architecture.

q: Richard Morris Hunt designed 'Marble House' (1888–1892), a lavish marble-clad mansion in the Beaux-Arts style, located in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Marble
n: Hunt's Marble House stands in Newport, Rhode Island, and is one of the grandest Beaux-Arts 'summer cottages' built for the Vanderbilt family.

q: Saint Peter's Church in Rome, whose dome was completed across roughly which span of years?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: Construction and the dome of Saint Peter's Church spanned roughly 1505 to the mid-1600s, a major project of Renaissance and early Baroque architecture.

q: San Vitale, completed around AD 546 in brick with a famous octagonal plan and mosaics of Justinian and Theodora, belongs to which architectural tradition?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: San Vitale in Ravenna is a defining example of Byzantine architecture, built under Emperor Justinian's patronage.

q: The unreinforced concrete dome of the Pantheon in Rome, still the largest of its kind, dates to roughly which period?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: The Pantheon's dome (AD 118–125) remains the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, an engineering feat unmatched for centuries.

q: The Pantheon in Rome (AD 118–125), whose dome is the world's largest of its kind, was built primarily using which material?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Concrete
n: The Pantheon's dome was cast in unreinforced Roman concrete, using lighter aggregate toward the top to reduce weight, a feat unmatched for over a thousand years.

q: Gustave Eiffel's Eiffel Tower, an icon of cast- and wrought-iron engineering, was completed in Paris in which year?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Cast Iron
n: The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889 for the Paris World's Fair, showcasing the structural possibilities of iron on an unprecedented scale.

q: The Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine, whose massive coffered vaults still dominate the Roman Forum, was completed around which date?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Arch
n: Completed around AD 310, the Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine used huge concrete-and-arch vaulting that later inspired Renaissance architects.

q: Richard Rogers, working with Buro Happold, designed London's domed Millennium Dome, completed in which year?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: The Millennium Dome opened in London in 2000, engineered with structural firm Buro Happold as one of the largest domed structures of its time.

q: Which of these is a marble-faced Ancient Roman building, completed roughly five centuries after the Acropolis's Golden Age?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Marble
n: The Pantheon (AD 118–125) postdates the Athenian Acropolis's mid-400s BC marble buildings by roughly five to six centuries, both being major marble monuments of the ancient world.

q: The Borgund Stave Church, an early wooden church known for its tiered, dragon-headed roofline, is located in which country?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Wood
n: Built roughly 1125–1150 in Sogn, Norway, Borgund is one of the best-preserved of Norway's medieval stave churches, built almost entirely of wood.

q: The Temple of Athena Nike, a small Ionic temple on the Acropolis of Athens, dates to roughly which period?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Column
n: The Temple of Athena Nike, completed around 425 BC, is a compact Ionic temple on the Athenian Acropolis, later than but near the Parthenon.

q: Filippo Brunelleschi's dome for Florence Cathedral, engineered without traditional wooden centering, was completed in which decade?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: Brunelleschi completed his self-supporting brick-ribbed dome for Florence Cathedral in the 1420s, one of the great engineering achievements of the early Renaissance.

q: The Great Mosque at Cordoba, famous for its forest of horseshoe arches, was begun in which year?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Arch
n: Begun in 785, the Great Mosque at Cordoba in Spain is renowned for its double-tiered horseshoe arches, a masterpiece of Islamic Architecture.

q: Alvar Aalto's brick Baker House dormitory (1947–1949), famous for its undulating riverside facade, was built for which institution?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: Aalto designed Baker House for MIT in Boston, using a curved brick wall and varied brick coloring to give the long dormitory a more organic, less monolithic form.

q: Joseph Paxton's Crystal Palace, an enormous cast-iron-and-glass exhibition hall, was built in 1851 to host which event?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Cast Iron
n: Paxton's Crystal Palace was erected in London for the Great Exhibition of 1851, a huge prefabricated cast-iron-and-glass structure built in a matter of months.

q: The brick city of Mohenjo Daro, built around 2600 BC, belonged to which civilization?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: Mohenjo Daro was a major city of the Indus Valley Civilization, known for its standardized fired-brick construction and grid street plan.

q: The Pont du Gard, a tall multi-tiered stone arch aqueduct, was built by the Romans near which French city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Arch
n: The Pont du Gard, dating to the late 100s BC, carried water toward Nimes and remains one of the best-preserved examples of Ancient Roman arch engineering.

q: Jorn Utzon's Sydney Opera House, completed in 1973 with its distinctive concrete-shell roofs, is located in which country?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Concrete
n: The Sydney Opera House, designed by Danish architect Jorn Utzon, used precast concrete shell segments to achieve its famous sail-like roofline.

q: The Acropolis of Athens, home to the marble Parthenon, reached its most famous building phase in roughly which period?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Marble
n: The Athenian Acropolis's major marble building campaign, including the Parthenon, dates to the mid-400s BC under Pericles.

q: Auguste Perret's Apartment at 25 bis Rue Franklin (1903), an early reinforced-concrete-frame residential building, is located in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Concrete
n: Perret's apartment building in Paris is considered one of the first major residential buildings to expose and celebrate a reinforced-concrete structural frame.

q: Abraham Darby III's Severn River Bridge, the world's first major cast-iron bridge, was completed in 1779 near which English location?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Cast Iron
n: Darby's bridge at Coalbrookdale, England, completed in 1779, was the first large-scale bridge built of cast iron, opening the door to iron-frame construction.

q: The Millennium Dome in London, completed in 2000, was engineered in collaboration with which structural firm?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Concrete
n: Richard Rogers worked with structural engineers Buro Happold on the Millennium Dome, whose tensioned fabric roof is supported by a ring of masts and cables.

q: The Great Temple of Amun at Karnak, known for its immense hypostyle hall of columns, is located near which modern city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Column
n: Built roughly 1295–1186 BC, the Great Temple of Amun at Karnak features one of the largest columned halls ever constructed, a hallmark of Ancient Egyptian Architecture.

q: Stonehenge, the famous stone circle in England, was constructed over roughly what span of time?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Stone
n: Stonehenge was built in phases from about 3100 BC to 1500 BC, making it a long-term prehistoric monument rather than a single quick construction.

q: Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed the great colonnaded piazza in front of which building, completed around the 1650s?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Column
n: Bernini's sweeping elliptical colonnade for Saint Peter's piazza in Rome (1650s) is a landmark of Baroque architecture, using paired columns to embrace the square.

q: The brick ziggurats of ancient Mesopotamia, dating to around 2000 BC, are associated with which culture?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: Ziggurats were massive stepped brick temple platforms built by the Sumerians, a hallmark of Ancient Near Eastern religious architecture.

q: Hendrik Petrus Berlage designed the brick Amsterdam Stock Exchange, completed in 1903, in a style that influenced which later movement?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: Berlage's honest use of exposed brick at the Amsterdam Stock Exchange (1903) is widely seen as a forerunner of the expressive Amsterdam School of architecture.

q: Charles Garnier's Paris Opera, completed in the 1860s and using cast iron in parts of its structure, was built in which architectural style?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Cast Iron
n: Garnier's opulent Paris Opera House, completed in the 1860s, is a defining monument of the Beaux-Arts style, blending iron construction with lavish stone and sculptural decoration.

q: Santa Maria de Quintanilla de las Vinas, a small stone church with horseshoe-arch influences, is located in which country?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Arch
n: Dating to the late 600s, this church near Burgos, Spain, is an example of Early Medieval Architecture that shows influence from Visigothic building traditions.

q: Henri Labrouste's cast-iron-framed Reading Room of the Bibliotheque Sainte-Genevieve, from the 1840s, is located in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Cast Iron
n: Labrouste's reading room in Paris exposed its slender cast-iron columns and arches, an influential early use of iron in a major public building.

q: The Palace of Darius at Persepolis, famous for its tall, slender columns, was built in which ancient region?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Column
n: Built around 518–460 BC, the palace at Persepolis stands in Iran and reflects the grand columned halls of Ancient Near Eastern royal architecture.

q: The Taj Mahal, famed for its white marble mausoleum, was built in Agra between roughly which years?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Marble
n: The Taj Mahal was constructed 1632–1648 in Agra, India, as a Mughal-era mausoleum and a masterpiece of Indian Architecture in white marble.

q: Frank Lloyd Wright's Kaufmann House, better known as Fallingwater, features dramatic reinforced-concrete cantilevers and is located in which state?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Concrete
n: Built in the 1930s in Mill Run, Pennsylvania, Fallingwater's concrete balconies cantilever directly over a waterfall, one of Wright's most celebrated designs.

q: Walter Gropius designed an Architect's House featuring extensive glass walls in 1938, in which English city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Glass
n: Gropius, who had earlier pioneered glass curtain walls at the Fagus Shoe Factory, designed this glass-forward Architect's House in Lincoln, England, in 1938.

q: Which structure used engaged columns as part of one of the earliest large-scale stone monumental complexes in history, at Saqqara?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Column
n: Djoser's funerary complex at Saqqara, c. 2665 BC, incorporated some of the earliest known engaged stone columns in monumental architecture.

q: The Forbidden City Complex, one of the largest surviving wooden palace complexes, was built primarily between roughly which years?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Wood
n: The Forbidden City in Beijing was developed mainly during the Ming dynasty, roughly 1368 to 1644, and relies heavily on timber-frame construction.

q: Frank Lloyd Wright's brick Frederick C. Robie House (1906–1909), a landmark of the Prairie School, is located in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: The Robie House, built in Chicago, is celebrated for its long horizontal brick lines, cantilevered roofs, and open interior planning typical of Wright's Prairie style.

q: Henry Hobson Richardson's Marshall Field Warehouse, an influential cast-iron-framed commercial building from the 1880s, was built in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Cast Iron
n: Richardson's Marshall Field Warehouse in Chicago combined a heavy masonry exterior with cast-iron interior framing, influencing the later Chicago School of skyscraper design.

q: Eero Saarinen designed the St. Louis Gateway Arch, completed in the 1960s, using which structural form for its shape?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Arch
n: Saarinen's Gateway Arch in St. Louis, Missouri, follows a catenary curve, the naturally efficient arch shape formed by a hanging chain.

q: Which structure at Saqqara is associated with early Ancient Egyptian building, though it is more famous for its columns than its arches?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Arch
n: Djoser's complex at Saqqara (c. 2665 BC) predates the widespread structural use of the true arch and instead relied on post-and-lintel and engaged-column construction.

q: The Lion Gate at Mycenae, an early monumental stone gateway using a relieving arch technique, dates to roughly which period?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Arch
n: The Lion Gate, from around 1250 BC, is a major example of Ancient Aegean Architecture and one of the earliest surviving monumental gateways in Europe.

q: Antoni Gaudi's Cathedral of Sagrada Familia, begun in 1884 and famous for its catenary-arch structural system, is located in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Arch
n: Gaudi began the Sagrada Familia in Barcelona in 1884; the building remains famous (and, notably, still unfinished for over a century) for its organically shaped arches and vaults.

q: Andrea Palladio designed the Villa Rotonda near Vicenza in the 1560s, a building celebrated for its use of what classical feature on all four facades?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Column
n: The Villa Rotonda's four identical porticoed facades, each with classical columns, made it one of the most influential designs of the Renaissance and later Palladian architecture worldwide.

q: The Funerary Complex of Djoser at Saqqara, an early large-scale stone complex with engaged columns, dates to roughly which period?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Column
n: Djoser's funerary complex, built around 2665 BC, is a landmark of Ancient Egyptian Architecture and one of the earliest monumental stone building projects.

q: Which pair of Pier Luigi Nervi buildings both used reinforced concrete, one a dome-roofed sports venue and one an earlier stadium?
o: Palazzetto dello Sport and Stadio Artemio Franchi
Sydney Opera House and the Eiffel Tower
Crystal Palace and the Millennium Dome
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Concrete
n: Nervi designed both the Stadio Artemio Franchi (1931) in Florence and the Palazzetto dello Sport (1959) in Rome, both celebrated for expressive reinforced-concrete structural forms.

q: Pier Luigi Nervi's Stadio Artemio Franchi, an early example of expressive reinforced-concrete stadium design from 1931, is located in which Italian city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Concrete
n: Nervi's stadium in Florence, completed in 1931, showcased his skill at shaping reinforced concrete into slender, structurally efficient forms.

q: The brick Fagus Shoe Factory (1911), known for its glass-curtain-wall corners, was designed by Walter Gropius together with whom?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: Gropius designed the Fagus Shoe Factory in Alfeld an der Leine, Germany, with Adolf Meyer; its glass curtain walls are considered a precursor of Bauhaus modernism.

q: Andrea Palladio's domed Villa Rotonda, built in the 1560s near Vicenza, later inspired which broader architectural movement?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: The Villa Rotonda's centralized, domed plan became the model for Palladianism, an influential classical style adopted across Europe and colonial America.

q: Pier Luigi Nervi's domed Palazzetto dello Sport in Rome, completed in 1959, was notable for its innovative use of which material?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: Nervi's Palazzetto dello Sport used a distinctive ribbed, thin-shell reinforced-concrete dome, showcasing his structural engineering expertise.

q: Who engineered the brick-ribbed dome of Florence Cathedral, completed in the 1420s without traditional wooden centering?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Brick
n: Filippo Brunelleschi (c. 1377–1446) devised an ingenious herringbone brick-laying pattern that let the dome self-support as it rose, a landmark feat of Renaissance engineering.

q: The Abbey at Montecassino, a marble building rebuilt many times over the centuries, is located in which country?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Marble
n: Montecassino, associated with Romanesque Architecture around the 1200s in its rebuilding phase, is a historic abbey in Italy.

q: The Pantheon in Rome, faced partly in marble and famous for its unreinforced concrete dome, dates to roughly which years?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Marble
n: The Pantheon was built roughly AD 118–125 under Emperor Hadrian; its interior combines marble facing with a massive concrete dome.

q: The Oklahoma State Capitol finally received its dome in which year, decades after the building itself was completed?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 33 — Dome
n: The Oklahoma State Capitol in Oklahoma City was completed without a dome for decades, finally gaining one in 2002.

q: Joseph Strauss led the engineering of the Golden Gate Bridge, completed in 1937, in which city?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 32 — Arch
n: Strauss oversaw the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco, whose towering steel arch-like suspension towers made it an engineering landmark of its era.
